transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-02-25 08:00 PT
- Duration: 46 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Steadfast Head of ML), Jenna Ortiz (Infra), Omar Rahman (CTO)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on per-token unit economics, where Steadfast wants to route inference across hosted/dedicated instances, track token burn and keep monthly cloud spend under a hard cap. They run a mix of short prompt retrieval + long-context summarization for logistics manifests, so batching and KV cache behavior matter.

Topics:
- Current stack and constraints (on-prem data, VPC needs)
- Budget ceiling and SLO tradeoffs (latency vs burn)
- Routing rules: region/cost/availability
- Pilot and benchmarking next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Um, quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the inference team and with me is Priya, our systems SE.
[00:07] Priya Rao: hi all, Priya — I focus on perf, batching and deployment options.
[00:11] Marcus Lee: Marcus here, head of ML. We run inference for route-sheets and manifest summarization, around 20% long form prompts.
[00:17] Jenna Ortiz: Jenna, infra. We're responsible for network egress, vpc peering and compliance.
[00:21] Omar Rahman: Omar, CTO. High level question first — can Redwood help us stay under a $60k/mo inference cap while keeping p95 latency under 350ms for short prompts?
[00:33] Alex Chen: good question. Short answer: likely, with a mix of hosted for spikes and dedicated for predictable baseline. We'll need to nail expected QPS and token distribution.
[00:42] Marcus Lee: right, QPS is spiky — baseline 120 qps, bursts to 2k during routing cutoffs. Our prompts: 70% < 120 tokens, the rest average ~1.8k tokens.
[00:55] Priya Rao: that mix matters a lot — few long requests kill batching efficiency. We recommend KV cache for repeated session context; that reduces per-token compute for long chats.
[01:05] Jenna Ortiz: just to be clear, we're not doing on-prem full hosting yet. We need VPC with private peering and keys in our KMS. Is that supported?
[01:14] Alex Chen: yes, Redwood Private via VPC is supported; you can bring your KMS/HSM and we provide audit logs. For pilot we can do a VPC peered hosted setup or a Dedicated pool in your region.
[01:24] Omar Rahman: what's the per-token delta between hosted and dedicated generally? ballpark.
[01:29] Priya Rao: rough rule — hosted per-token price is higher but includes multi-tenant infra and auto-fallbacks. Dedicated reduces per-token compute cost because you amortize GPUs, maybe 25-45% cheaper per token depending on model and batching. But you pay for reserved capacity commit.
[01:44] Marcus Lee: if the drop is up to 45% that would be huge, but we can't overcommit. How does burst capacity work?
[01:50] Alex Chen: Dedicated has burst windows you can configure; you pick a baseline reserved and allow controlled burst to hosted capacity. Billing shows token split across hosted and dedicated so you can see the unit economics.
[02:02] Jenna Ortiz: what about prefix caching? we have lots of repeated headers in manifests.
[02:07] Priya Rao: prefix/KV cache is big — for repeated prefixes we hit the KV store and skip recomputation for many tokens. That can drop compute cost dramatically for your workload. The caveat: long-context items still incur memory for KV but per-token compute is lower.
[02:22] Marcus Lee: our manifests reuse the same route headers 60% of the time, so sounds promising. Any architectural constraints to enable that?
[02:28] Priya Rao: would need session affinity and a small amount of warmed-kv state. On hosted we can do it automatically for a session key if you send it; on Dedicated you have more control over cache residency and you can pin warm caches to GPU instances.
[02:41] Omar Rahman: okay, let's get into specifics — we have a fixed $60k/mo. What levers should we move to stay inside that?
[02:49] Alex Chen: three levers — model choice/size, batching settings, and caching/affinity. Also routing policies: send latency-sensitive short prompts to hosted for lower cold-start and send bulk summarization to dedicated where you can batch more.
[03:02] Priya Rao: to quantify: if you run a 7B model on dedicated with good batching and KV cache you might get per-token compute cost of X (placeholder, but lower) vs hosted which is Y. We usually run a micro-benchmark to give numbers.
[03:13] Marcus Lee: what's X vs Y numerically? we need to show finance.
[03:16] Priya Rao: we should run your exact prompt mix — but a sample: hosted gen cost say $0.00045/token for a certain model vs dedicated effective $0.00026/token after amortizing reserved GPU. These are example values — we'll benchmark.
[03:29] Jenna Ortiz: are there other hidden costs — egress, audit logs?
[03:33] Alex Chen: audit logs, higher retention is an add-on. Egress depends on region but you control peering. We'll include those in the pricing sheet.
[03:42] Marcus Lee: on routing — is automated fallback possible? like if dedicated capacity is saturated, fall back to hosted seamlessly?
[03:49] Priya Rao: yes, smart routing supports rules by latency/cost/region. You can set thresholds and Redwood will transparently fallback to a compatible model variant on hosted. That does increase per-token cost for those requests but keeps the app up.
[04:02] Omar Rahman: in terms of SLA, can you meet p95 350ms on short prompts? That depends on region and whether we use hosted or dedicated.
[04:11] Priya Rao: for short prompts under 120 tokens, hosted in the same region with optimized kernels can hit p95 ~200-300ms. Dedicated typically better for stable low latency if you provision for the baseline. But remember batching increases throughput at cost of slight added latency — we tune batch windows.
[04:29] Marcus Lee: what's the smallest commit for Dedicated to see the 30% savings?
[04:33] Alex Chen: it depends on model and your target throughput. For your baseline ~120 qps, a small dedicated cluster (like one mid-tier multi-GPU pool) might be enough — we'll model it in the pilot pricing.
[04:45] Jenna Ortiz: security checks — SOC2, SSO, RBAC, and ability to do on-prem connectors.
[04:52] Alex Chen: Redwood has SOC 2, supports SAML SSO, RBAC, and Private deployments allow air-gapped/on-prem installations. We'll attach security docs.
[05:01] Priya Rao: also note quantization options — 4-bit models reduce memory and cost but sometimes affect quality. For manifest summarization we saw minimal regression at 4-bit fine tuned variants, but we'll validate on your eval set.
[05:14] Marcus Lee: okay, evaluation — we want a pilot that shows: baseline cost projection, latencies p50/p95, and a sample of quality metrics for summarization. Can you do that within three weeks?
[05:25] Alex Chen: Yes, typical pilot timeline is 2-4 weeks. We'll run a small dedicated baseline + hosted fallback, synthetic load replay and your sample traffic to measure key numbers.
[05:36] Jenna Ortiz: how intrusive is the integration — SDKs or direct REST?
[05:40] Priya Rao: both — SDKs for quick integration, REST for direct calls. For VPC we do private endpoints and a small sidecar to forward traffic if needed.
[05:49] Marcus Lee: on telemetry — we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards to see where burn happens.
[05:55] Alex Chen: Redwood Console gives token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and per model. We'll enable your team access for the pilot.
[06:03] Omar Rahman: ok good. Now some quick objections from finance — what if, after pilot, the dedicated commit doesn't hit expected savings? How do we fail safe?
[06:12] Alex Chen: we build in a canary phase and you can keep low commit levels initially. There's also automatic fallback and you can scale out or down monthly. Contracts have exit windows for annual commitments.
[06:22] Priya Rao: plus we can run a sensitivity analysis during pilot showing where the breakpoint is — e.g., if average tokens per request drop or bursts increase, how the per-token break-even shifts.
[06:34] Marcus Lee: fine. A few practical clarifications: 1) will we get raw logs for debugging? 2) can we pin specific model versions? 3) how are token boundaries defined when we pre-tokenize?
[06:46] Priya Rao: 1) yes, logs and traces for your routes; 2) yes, model pinning and rollout controls; 3) we count tokens per the model tokenizer (we'll show tokenization examples), but you can pre-tokenize and send token counts for billing reconciliation.
[07:00] Jenna Ortiz: and peak protection — do you have surge protection for the 2k qps windows?
[07:04] Alex Chen: yes, burst capacity and throttling policies. You can set routing priority so core transactions get priority.
[07:12] Marcus Lee: ok I think we have enough to move forward. Can you summarize next steps?
[07:16] Alex Chen: sure. I'll send a pilot pricing sheet with three hosting mixes and a recommended dedicated baseline. Priya will share a bench checklist and KV cache configuration notes. Marcus/Jenna will export a 7-day anonymized request profile and target SLOs.
[07:29] Omar Rahman: timeline for those docs?
[07:32] Alex Chen: we'll aim to have the pricing and checklist to you by Monday 2026-03-02. Pilot kickoff earliest the following week assuming you sign the pilot quote.
[07:42] Marcus Lee: sounds good. One more thing — competitors: we also looked at Bedrock and Anthropic — main tie-breaker is observability and cost transparency.
[07:52] Alex Chen: understood, we'll include clear unit-econ breakdowns and an exportable dashboard for finance.
[07:58] Jenna Ortiz: thanks everyone.
[08:01] Priya Rao: thanks — we'll follow up with the checklist.
[08:04] Alex Chen: thanks, bye.
